name: Whitening mouthwash

image.caption: COLGATE 500 ML PŁYN DO PŁUKANIA UST PLAX MOUTHWASH WHITENING EAN

lead: Whitening mouthwashes are daily rinses used to gradually lighten teeth or limit new staining as part of a routine. Some contain low-level hydrogen peroxide, others non-peroxide agents.

They act through brief contact during rinsing, which is short compared with strips or trays. Wikipedia describes use twice daily for one minute, with visible results possibly taking up to three months. Published work found is laboratory-based; no clinical studies were found.

paras: People swish for about a minute, usually twice a day, alongside brushing, and keep it up for weeks to months. It is often combined with whitening toothpaste or periodic professional treatment.
Laboratory studies have examined alcohol-containing rinses for effects on enamel, dentine and restorative materials. In the EU, retail products are limited to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide.

angle.text: Whitening mouthwash is used daily to gradually lighten teeth or limit new stain, through brief contact with peroxide or non-peroxide agents. Research on these products so far is laboratory-based.

lead: Whitening mouthwashes are rinses sold to lighten teeth or lift surface stains with daily use. Some contain hydrogen peroxide at low concentrations and others rely on non-peroxide agents such as charcoal. People use them as the lowest-effort step in a whitening routine: a one-minute rinse added to brushing, aimed at a brighter smile without trays or strips.[1]

Wikipedia describes whitening rinses as used twice daily for one minute, with visible results possibly taking up to three months, and notes that in the EU retail products may contain up to 0.1% hydrogen peroxide.[1] Because contact time is brief compared with strips, trays or in-office gels, rinses are usually discussed as a maintenance or add-on product.

Published work is mostly laboratory-based, using extracted teeth and resin or ceramic restorations stained with coffee, though a few small clinical comparisons exist. Studies have measured colour change, surface roughness and hardness after simulated months or years of rinsing.[2][3][4][5][6][7][8]
infobox: Listerine Whitening, Listerine Advanced White, Colgate Max White, Oral-B 3D White Luxe, iWhite[4][15]
Mostly in vitro; few small clinical comparisons

paras: Whitening rinses fall into two broad groups. Peroxide-based rinses deliver a small amount of hydrogen peroxide, the same oxidiser used in strips and gels at far higher strengths. Non-peroxide rinses use other ingredients, including activated charcoal in some newer products, and are marketed to lift or prevent surface stain rather than bleach the tooth interior.[4][5]

Wikipedia's tooth whitening article states that whitening works when oxygen sources such as hydrogen peroxide react with stains on or inside the tooth, and that peroxide diffuses into the tooth and breaks into free radicals that fragment pigment molecules so they reflect less light.[1] For comparison, it reports in-office gels at roughly 3 to 16% hydrogen peroxide equivalent and EU retail products capped at 0.1%, with 0.1 to 6% reserved for products supplied by dental professionals.[1] A mouthwash, which is in contact with teeth for about a minute, delivers a small fraction of the exposure of a tray or strip.

People who want whiter teeth often stack products: whitening toothpaste, strips and a rinse. Rinses are popular for convenience, as they require no fitted tray and add little time and fit into an existing brushing routine. Wikipedia notes that visible results may take up to three months of regular use.[1]

Colour change is usually quantified in research with spectrophotometers, using the CIE lightness value L* and the colour-difference metric delta E; differences of roughly 1.8 delta E00 are described in one study as the 50:50 acceptability threshold for visible discolouration in resin composite.[9]

An in vitro study assessed whether a hydrogen-peroxide-based mouthwash alters enamel colour,[3] and a laboratory paper examined the efficacy of mouthwashes containing hydrogen peroxide on tooth whitening.[10] Another study evaluated four non-peroxide rinses on forty incisors over four weeks, measuring colour with a digital spectrophotometer.[4] A laboratory study tested a charcoal-containing toothpaste and mouthwash on coffee-stained canines over a simulated 90 days.[5]

For stained resin composite, a 12-month in vitro study of six whitening mouthwashes found that all but one reduced colour change below the acceptability threshold, with the fastest product reaching it after one month and others after about three months.[9] A separate comparison of whitening methods on stained CAD/CAM polymer materials found home bleaching removed more stain and resisted re-staining better, while the mouthwash increased lightness by roughly 2 units across materials.[11] A study of different whitening agents on resin composites likewise reported that at-home and in-office agents produced greater colour change than a whitening mouthwash, pen, toothpaste or pre-filled tray.[12]

Laboratory studies have examined alcohol-containing mouthwashes including Listerine Whitening on enamel and restorative materials. A simulation of up to six months of daily use reported no relevant changes in surface morphology under scanning electron microscopy or in calcium and phosphorus content of enamel.[2] A dentine study examined erosion from a whitening mouthwash combined with toothbrushing abrasion,[6] and another examined surface hardness and colour stability of nanohybrid resin composite after different mouthwashes.[7]

Simulated rinsing of CAD/CAM restorative materials, representing 15 years of use, found that a feldspathic ceramic and a polymer-infiltrated ceramic network became brighter, more opaque, less glossy and rougher after whitening mouthwash.[13] The CAD/CAM comparison also reported increased roughness in two of the materials tested.[11] A further study examined bleaching mouthwash and force decay of orthodontic elastomeric chains.[8] Wikipedia lists tooth sensitivity, gum irritation and effects on restorations among the general side effects of peroxide whitening, at far higher concentrations than a rinse delivers.[1]

A randomised, double-blind, parallel-group trial reported in the American Journal of Dentistry compared a hydrogen peroxide strip regimen with a peroxide-free regimen of strips, toothpaste and whitening mouthwash from one brand. Of 50 adults randomised, 48 completed the trial, and tooth colour was measured by digital image analysis after 7, 10 and 14 treatments.[14] The rinse was part of a multi-product regimen, so the trial does not isolate the mouthwash.

A comparison of low-concentration home bleaching products (a whitening strip, a gel and a mouthwash) used clinical and digital quantitative light-induced fluorescence methods to assess stain removal.[15] Apart from these, studies of whitening mouthwashes are laboratory-based.

timeline.event: A pyrozone mouthwash is reported to have reduced cavities and whitened teeth.[1]
Custom tray bleaching is introduced, later favouring carbamide peroxide.[1]
Whitening strips appear, the format that later retail rinses and toothpastes were compared against.[1]
